query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting the heavy Hf component in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with a lighter refractory element (e.g., Nb) will lower the alloy’s overall density while preserving its room‐temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with high density (~10.21 g/cm³), ~1600 MPa room‐temperature yield strength, and ~855 MPa yield strength at elevated temperature (~1000 °C).
generation.intervention: Replace a significant fraction (e.g., ~75% of the atomic fraction) of Hf with Nb to form a modified composition, for example Hf0.25MoTaTiZr supplemented by Nb (switching to a Hf–Nb–Mo–Ta–Ti–Zr system).
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing performed at room temperature under quasi‐static tensile/compression loading and at 1000 °C under similar loading rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The modified local solid‐solution structure should maintain fine grain size and lattice distortion levels similar to the as‐cast state, ensuring comparable solid solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Substituting Hf with Nb reduces the alloy’s density due to Nb’s lower atomic mass while retaining or even enhancing solid solution strengthening and grain refinement. Prior evidence suggests that smaller proportions of Hf may favorably influence strength, and Nb is known to provide good ductility and strength, helping maintain performance at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new alloy is predicted to show a significant reduction in density (closer to densities in the 8–9 g/cm³ range) while maintaining room‐temperature yield strengths near 1600 MPa and 1000 °C yield strengths around 850 MPa. There is an expectation of retaining high ductility (over 50%) at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr: density ~10.21 g/cm³, ~1600 MPa room‐temperature yield strength, ~855 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C, and high ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The intervention is considered within the processing window of as‐cast alloy production and under quasi‐static mechanical loading conditions at ambient temperature and 1000 °C. Deviations outside these conditions may not hold the predicted property balance.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative effects on yield strength and ductility may vary with processing details and precise compositional ratios. While prior molecular dynamics and experimental studies support benefits of reduced Hf content, the trade‐offs in the specific multiprincipal alloy system require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a set of alloys with graded partial substitutions of Hf by Nb (e.g., 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% Hf replaced) using the same as‐cast processing route. Measure density, microstructure (grain size and phase purity), and mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile/compression tests to determine yield strength and ductility
High-temperature mechanical tests at 1000 °C to assess yield strength
Microstructural characterization (optical/electron microscopy) to verify grain size and phase consistency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with partial Hf substitution by Nb does not achieve a statistically significant reduction in density (targeting a reduction of at least ~10-15%) or if its yield strengths at either room temperature or 1000 °C drop by more than 10% relative to the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
High-entropy alloy (HEA) is a new type of multi-principal alloy material and the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr HEAs have attracted more and more attention from researchers due to their high melting point, special plasticity, and excellent corrosion resistance. In this paper, in order to reduce the density of the alloy and maintain the strength of the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr HEAs, the effects of high-density elements Hf and Ta on the properties of HEAs were explored for the first time based on molecular dynamics simulations. A low-density and high-strength Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr HEA suitable for laser melting deposition was designed and formed. Studies have shown that the decrease in the proportion of Ta element reduces the strength of HEA, while the decrease in Hf element increases the strength of HEA. The simultaneous decrease in the ratio of Hf and Ta elements reduces the elastic modulus and strength of HEA and leads to the coarsening of the alloy microstructure. The application of laser melting deposition (LMD) technology refines the grains and effectively solves the coarsening problem. ## Abstract
AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
